spans.t: This is a small book for twelve days. It is made to go with the Camino Portugués from Porto, a road of about two weeks and ~240 km, with a day or two to spare for rest and rain. Read one day for each day of walking, or one a day at home, and nobody will mind if you skip one, repeat one, or save a day for a rest day.
The Pilgrim's Progress

was written by John Bunyan in the seventeenth century, and it is an allegory of a pilgrimage: a story in which every road, house and traveller stands for something else. Its hero, Christian, sets out from the City of Destruction with a heavy burden, and the book follows him, place by place, to the gate of a distant city. That is why it fits any road, and not only this one. It is a story about what a long walk does to a person: the weight, the bog, the borrowed comfort, the hill, the fright, the wrong turning, the company, the river.
Every day has a morning reading of about five minutes and an evening reflection of about three.
In the morning
there are three parts.

items.t: The passage.
A short stretch of Bunyan's own words, copied exactly from the public-domain text of the first part of his book, old spelling and old grammar and all.
Thee
and
thou
and
hath

are there. Read the passage twice, the second time aloud if you can, even under your breath. Old English slows the eye down, and that is half its use. Speakers in the story are marked as the edition marks them, by short labels such as
CHR.
for Christian.
The reflection.

This part is ours, not Bunyan's. It starts from something on the road, a strap, a stile, a bench, and lets the passage open it. It says what the passage says, where it is hard, and what it might ask of an ordinary day. It is allowed to doubt.
For the walk.
A question to carry for the next hour and one small practice that needs nothing but attention. Most of them are better done on your feet.

spans.t: In the evening
there are two more.

items.t: At the end of the day.
A look back at the day you have lived, with the morning's passage in mind, and two or three questions to lie down with. You do not need to write anything.
A short prayer.
Original and short. If you pray, pray it. If you pray differently, change the words. If you do not pray, say it as a wish, to nobody in particular.

spans.t: A Christian book, and who it is for
The Pilgrim's Progress

is a Christian book, of a strongly Protestant kind, and it takes sin, judgement and hell more seriously than most readers do today. We say so plainly so that nobody is surprised. People walk the Camino for many reasons: faith, sport, grief, curiosity, a rest from work. All of them are welcome here. You do not need to believe what Bunyan believed to recognise the bog, the hill, the wrong turning and the river. Where the book is hard, we say so, and the next chapter says what we have left out.
The shape of the twelve days
The days follow the story in its own order, from the first page to the last.

items.t: Days 1 to 4, setting out.
The burden, the bog, the gate, and the hill that follows the cross.
Days 5 to 8, the middle of the road.
A house that takes pilgrims in, a valley of humility, a valley of darkness, and a fair where everything is for sale.
Days 9 to 12, trouble and arrival.
A smooth path that goes wrong, a high place with a view, a drowsy country, and a river.

spans.t: The shape is a shape, not a timetable. The book cannot know which day of your walk is the hard one. Read the day that fits the day you are having. If you are tired, read the passage and the prayer and leave the rest for the morning.
On the road and at home

Read the morning part on a bench, in a bunk, in a café while the soup arrives. Then put the phone away and take the question with you for an hour. Read the evening part last of all, when the boots are off. At home it works the same way: the morning with your tea, the evening before bed.
Two words you will meet.
Albergue
is the simple hostel where pilgrims sleep, often in bunks, often with a communal kitchen.
Buen Camino
is what walkers say to one another on the road, roughly, may your Way go well. Other words are explained where they first appear.

chapters.title: About the book and its author

spans.t: The man

John Bunyan was born in 1628 at Elstow, near Bedford in England, and died in 1688. He was a tinker, a mender of pots and pans, and later a preacher in Bedford, among the Protestants who would not conform to the Church of England and were punished for it in his day. The file we use says none of this: these are well-known facts, which we could not check in the text itself. He was jailed in Bedford for preaching without leave, and he is usually said to have written the first part of this book in prison, though scholars differ about which imprisonment, the long one that began in about 1660 or a shorter one in the mid-1670s. The book was first printed in 1678.
The book
The Pilgrim's Progress

is an allegory, a story in which every person and place stands for something else, and Bunyan tells it as a dream. In the opening lines he lies down in a "Den" and dreams. The edition we use carries the full title
The Pilgrim's Progress from this world to that which is to come

, and the words "delivered under the similitude of a dream". It begins with a verse apology, in which Bunyan explains with some humour why he wrote it, and ends with a verse conclusion, which asks the reader to look "within my veil" for what is useful.

The edition holds the first part only. A note at its head says that Bunyan wrote a sequel some years afterwards, and that the first part is "a complete work in itself". The sequel is not here, and we do not quote it. The first part follows one man, Christian, from the City of Destruction to the gate of the Celestial City, with a companion, Faithful, for part of the way, and another, Hopeful, for the rest. The places he passes have names that say what they are: the Slough of Despond, the Hill Difficulty, the Valley of Humiliation, Vanity Fair, Doubting Castle, the Delectable Mountains, the Enchanted Ground.
Why it suits a pilgrim
Bunyan says it himself, in his apology:

paras.t: This book will make a traveller of thee, If by its counsel thou wilt ruled be; It will direct thee to the Holy Land, If thou wilt its directions understand: Yea, it will make the slothful active be; The blind also delightful things to see.

cite.t: , The Author's Apology for his Book (English original, 1678)

spans.t: It is a story of feet and weather, bad ground and good company, being lost and being found again. A man sinks in a bog, crawls up a hill, is taken in by strangers, and is held above water by a friend.
What is hard, and what we left out
It is also a severe book of its century, and we say what is hard so that you are not surprised by it in the original.

items.t: The burden Christian carries is, for Bunyan, the weight of sin and the fear of judgement, and the book takes hell as real. Christian leaves his wife and children when they will not come, and the first part does not make that easy.

Two places name the Pope as an enemy: a cave at the end of the Valley of the Shadow of Death, where two giants once lived, and a line about Rome in the description of Vanity Fair. A pilgrim walking to Santiago may well be Catholic and may wince. We left both out, and say so here instead of passing over them.

The Interpreter, a guide Christian meets early, shows him a man shut in an iron cage who says he cannot repent. Vanity Fair ends with a trial, a death and a burning. In Doubting Castle the giant urges his prisoners to kill themselves, and one of them refuses. The story ends on a man who came to the gate without the paper he needed, and who is taken away. We left out the cage, the burning and that ending, and we deal with the dungeon with care on Day 9.

spans.t: We took twelve short passages, one for each of twelve stretches of the road, from the narrative and the verse, and nothing from the notes the edition also carries. The order is Bunyan's own. The choosing, the reflections, the questions and the prayers are ours.
The edition and the licence
The text is
The Pilgrim's Progress

, by John Bunyan, in the original seventeenth-century English, prepared by Project Gutenberg volunteers and published there as ebook number 131. The file names no translator and no modern editor, and says nothing of a year. The date 1678 is the well-known date of the first part, not something the file tells us. The text is old enough to be in the public domain, and every quotation in this book was checked against it, word for word.

We changed nothing in the passages. We kept the old spellings, capitals and punctuation, and the labels that mark who speaks. The edition adds numbers in curly brackets between its paragraphs, Bible references in square brackets, and some short side notes. Those are not the story, and we did not copy them. Where a passage skips a stretch, or a note stood between two sentences, a mark like this shows it: …. Nothing of the Project Gutenberg licence text or trademark is copied here.
What are you carrying that does not show on the scales?
The passage

paras.t: As I walked through the wilderness of this world, I lighted on a certain place where was a Den, and I laid me down in that place to sleep: and, as I slept, I dreamed a dream. I dreamed, and behold, I saw a man clothed with rags, standing in a certain place, with his face from his own house, a book in his hand, and a great burden upon his back. … I looked, and saw him open the book, and read therein; and, as he read, he wept, and trembled; and, not being able longer to contain, he brake out with a lamentable cry, saying, "What shall I do?" … In this plight, therefore, he went home and refrained himself as long as he could, that his wife and children should not perceive his distress; but he could not be silent long, because that his trouble increased.

cite.t: , Part One, the opening of the dream, the City of Destruction (English original, 1678)

spans.t: Reflection

The first morning has a small ceremony of its own. You lift the pack, swing it onto your shoulders, tighten the straps until the weight sits on your hips and not on your neck, and take a first step out of a door that is not yours, in Porto or wherever your road begins. Somewhere in those few seconds you learn what you have really brought, and the kilos you packed are the smallest part of it.

Bunyan opens his book with a man who is carrying something he cannot put down. The book is an allegory, a story in which every person and place stands for something else, and Bunyan tells it as a dream. He lies down in a
Den

, falls asleep, and sees a man in rags, with his back to his own house, a book in his hand and a great burden on his back. The burden is not luggage. In Bunyan's story it is a person's guilt, and the fear of what comes after death, which the man has found by reading his book. Not every reader will share that fear, or put it that way. It is worth seeing what Bunyan does with it all the same, because he is shrewd about the human side.
The man opens the book and reads, and as he reads he weeps and trembles, and then he cries out,
What shall I do?

That is the whole first move of a pilgrimage: a plain question, said aloud. It is not a plan and it does not come with an answer. Many walks begin there, in a trouble that has outgrown the place where it was kept.

Notice, too, how Bunyan places him. He is standing with his face turned from his own house. He has not left yet. He has only turned round, and that is where most journeys really begin, a good while before the first step, in a turning of the head that nobody else can see.
Then comes a detail that is easy to read past. He goes home and holds himself in
as long as he could

, so that his wife and children will not see. Anyone who has carried a worry to the dinner table and talked about something else knows that sentence. When he can no longer hold it in he tells them, and they do not believe him. They decide that some fever has got into his head, and they put him to bed, hoping sleep will settle him. The night is as bad as the day.

Here is where the passage is harder than it looks, and we should say so. The passage stops before the man sets off, and when he does he runs, with his fingers in his ears, and leaves his family behind. Bunyan does not make that easy. Much later in the book a woman asks him why he did not bring them, and he weeps and says how gladly he would have done it. If you are walking away from people for a fortnight, you may find that this part of the story presses on a bruise. A phone call home is allowed.

There is a second hard thing. For Bunyan the burden is sin, and the danger behind the man is a city that will be burned. You may carry something quite different, a bereavement, a decision, a year of work that wore you down, a question you have not dared to ask, or nothing heavier than a wish for a different kind of day. The story does not need you to carry his burden. It only asks you to take seriously that you are carrying one. People set out on this road for many reasons, and some of them have no burden at all but curiosity. Bunyan's road has room for that too.

What does this ask of an ordinary first day? Mostly honesty about the weight. The pack you can check, on a scale or by the ache in your shoulders. The other weight you can only notice. It helps to know that you do not have to solve it today. Nothing in the story takes the burden off on the first page. It will be a long way before it falls, and Day 4 of this book comes to that. For now the job is smaller, and the man in the dream has already done it: stop, look at what is on your back, and say aloud that it is there.

And one doubt, because this book would rather be honest than soothing. Some days the burden is only a poor night's sleep, a tight hip and a lunch that was too far away. Not everything needs to be an allegory, and a day is allowed to be only a day.
For the walk

items.t: What am I carrying today that is not in the pack? Ask it once, lightly, and do not hunt for the answer.

At your first stop, loosen the straps and let the pack rest on the ground for a full minute. While it rests, name the other weight in one word, to yourself, and tell nobody. Then lift the pack again and notice whether it feels any different.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The boots come off, and the day makes its first honest report: where the strap bit, where a seam rubbed, which sock was a mistake. After a first day the body always has more to say than the mind, and it is worth listening before you do anything else. Air your feet, look for any spot that is hot or tender before it turns into a blister, drink some water, and eat something with salt in it. The questions below can wait ten minutes.

Think back to the question from the morning. Perhaps you did not give it a thought, and the road took all your attention: the signs, the feet, the next turning. That is not a failure, and it is a kind of rest. Perhaps it came and went, at a bench or in a long flat stretch, and each time it came it was a little smaller or a little larger than you expected. Either way, you now know something that you did not know at breakfast, which is how it feels to walk with it.

Bunyan's man, in the pages just after the passage, stands still in the field because he cannot tell which way to go. He looks this way and that as if he would run. That may be how this evening feels, to be out on the road without yet being sure why. It is allowed. In the story a stranger comes up, and he does not give the man a map. He points over a wide field and asks whether he can see a light, and says to keep that light in his eye. For the next two weeks a yellow arrow on a wall or a stone is the nearest thing to that, and nobody needs more than the next one.

There is also the matter of the people you left. Perhaps one of them crossed your mind today, in a village, on a bridge, at a table for one. It may be worth sending them a line tonight: two sentences, no more, to say where you slept. It costs little, and it can lighten the evening more than a hot shower. If nobody is waiting, a line in a notebook does the same job: a record that you were somewhere, on this date, and that you came through it.

One practical thing belongs here too. If the pack felt heavier than you hoped, tonight is the time to ask whether one item can go: sent home, given away, left on a shelf. The other weight cannot be posted anywhere, but it too can be shifted a little, just by admitting what it is.
Be gentle about tiredness. A first evening is the worst time to judge a road, because the body has not yet learned the work and the mind is trying to learn it all at once. If the answer to
what shall I do?
feels too large tonight, shrink it to what you can see: eat, wash, lie down. Tomorrow is a day's walk, not a verdict.

items.t: What did I carry today that I did not pack?
Whom did I think of, and is there one thing I would like them to know?
What is the smallest step I can take tomorrow morning?

spans.t: A short prayer
Tonight I set the pack down, and let the weight be what it is. I do not have to solve it before sleep. Show me tomorrow's first step, only that one. Keep the people I have left, and keep me.
When fear hurries you, what do you miss?
The passage

paras.t: Now I saw in my dream, that just as they had ended this talk they drew near to a very miry slough, that was in the midst of the plain; and they, being heedless, did both fall suddenly into the bog. The name of the slough was Despond. Here, therefore, they wallowed for a time, being grievously bedaubed with the dirt; and Christian, because of the burden that was on his back, began to sink in the mire. … HELP. But why did not you look for the steps? CHR. Fear followed me so hard, that I fled the next way, and fell in. HELP. Then said he, Give me thy hand: so he gave him his hand, and he drew him out, and set him upon sound ground, and bid him go on his way. … True, there are, by the direction of the Law-giver, certain good and substantial steps, placed even through the very midst of this slough; but at such time as this place doth much spew out its filth, as it doth against change of weather, these steps are hardly seen; or, if they be, men, through the dizziness of their heads, step beside, and then they are bemired to purpose, notwithstanding the steps be there; but the ground is good when they are once got in at the gate.

cite.t: , Part One, the Slough of Despond (English original, 1678)

spans.t: Reflection

By the second day the first-morning energy has gone, and what is left is the road as it really is. The legs are stiff in new places. The thing you were looking forward to has turned out to be mostly ground. Somewhere in the middle of the morning a small voice asks what you were thinking, and the odd thing is that it asks it when nothing in particular has gone wrong.

Bunyan has a place for that voice, and he gives it a name. Christian has set out with a neighbour, Pliable, who has been won over by talk of a better country. They are walking along in high spirits, describing its pleasures to each other, and they are
heedless
. The ground gives way, and they are both in a bog. It is called the Slough of Despond. A slough is a marsh, and to despond is to lose heart, so the name says exactly what the place does.

The first thing to notice is when it happens: at the height of the good talk, not the bottom of a bad day. A hopeful hour is no protection, and sometimes it is the very time the feet are least careful.
The second is how differently the two men take it. Pliable asks where Christian is now, and Christian answers truthfully that he does not know. Then Pliable turns on him:
Is this the happiness you have told me all this while of?

If this is how things go at the very start, he says, what will they be like by the end? With a struggle or two he gets out on the side nearest his own house, and goes home. Christian is left behind, still struggling in the mire because of his burden.

Then Help arrives, and the exchange that follows is short. He asks a question, not a scolding: why did you not look for the steps? Christian's answer is the truest line in the passage. Fear followed him so hard that he took the nearest way, and fell in. Fear hurries people. It makes the first path look like the only one, and it takes away the patience to look about for the one that was laid there for you. Help does not lecture. He says
Give me thy hand
, and Christian gives it.

The steps are the other thing to notice. Bunyan says there are good, sound steps placed right through the middle of the bog. But when the place is at its worst, in a change of weather, the steps are hard to see, and a tired, giddy head steps beside them. That is the rhythm of a bad patch on a long walk. The arrows are still there. A grey morning makes them harder to read, and a mind that is tired or frightened looks for any way out and not for the marked one.

Here is a practical way to read it. The steps are the plain things that do not depend on your mood: water, something to eat, a bench, a dry sock, the next waymark. They are not cures for despondency. They are only what is under your feet while you work out what you feel. When the ground goes soft, go to the plain steps first, and decide about everything else afterwards.

Now the hard part, and Bunyan is not gentle about it. Pliable, who goes home, is soon mocked by his neighbours for turning back, and later in the book he is held up as a warning. We do not need to take that over. On a road, turning back, cutting a stage short, taking a rest day or a bus to the next town are not disgraces, and sometimes they are the only sensible thing to do. The only caution in Bunyan's story that carries over is a quiet one: do not decide about the whole road in the middle of the bog. Decide on a dry day, after a meal and some sleep.

And where is Help? He is not guaranteed. The story has him walk up at the right moment, and a road does not always oblige. Sometimes help is a stranger, sometimes it is a message from home, sometimes only a wall to sit against. What Christian does that is within anyone's reach is the last thing: he puts out his hand. In a bog that may be the hardest step of all.
For the walk

items.t: Where did fear make me take the nearest way today, and not the next step?
When a doubt turns up, say
slough

quietly to yourself, the way you might name a bird. Then do the plainest step in sight: a drink of water, a sock straightened, a look for the next waymark. Treat the doubt as weather and the steps as ground.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The second evening is often the one on which the body sends in its first proper bill. A knee, a heel, a shoulder, a back that was fine yesterday: they will all want a word. Give them one before the questions, with water, a stretch and your feet up for a few minutes.

Think back to the moment today when the day tipped. Most days have one. It was not the hardest hour, probably, and it may not have had any special cause. It could have been a long stretch beside traffic, or the hour after lunch, or the first climb, or the point at which you realised how far you still had to go. A small, quiet voice said that this was a mistake. Bunyan has Pliable say it aloud, as if to someone else:
Is this the happiness you have told me all this while of?
It is worth asking who the
you
is. It may have been a friend who talked you into this road. More often it is the part of you that talked yourself into it, and that part deserves an answer before bed.
Then look for the steps. There may have been some that you took without noticing: a sit-down at the right time, a bite of food that cleared your head, a stranger's
Buen Camino

that came at the very moment you needed it. If you took none, and got through anyway, the day still had steps, only you did not see them. Either way it is useful to learn which ones work on you, because tomorrow's bog will be like today's.

A kind word for Pliable, whom Bunyan is hard on. He was not wicked. He was a man who found the going rougher than the talk. Most walkers have been Pliable at least once in an afternoon, and some have been Pliable for a whole morning and then got up and gone on. Bunyan is hard on him, and you need not be hard on yourself. Doubts are always larger in the evening, when the body has spent its sugar. A hard decision about the whole road does not belong on a bunk at nine o'clock at night. Eat first, sleep, and decide in the morning, if there is anything left to decide.

Bunyan makes a wry point in the same scene, in words we have not quoted. Help says that for ages labourers have been tipping cartloads of wholesome advice into the slough, and that it is a slough still. Advice does not drain despondency. If someone you walked beside today sank into a bog of their own, a hand will probably do more than a good reason, and a cup of something hot more than either.

items.t: When did the day tip into doubt today, and what was my body asking for at that moment?
Which plain steps did I take today, whether or not I noticed them?
Is there a hand that was offered to me today, in words or in kindness, that I did not take?

spans.t: A short prayer

When the ground goes soft under me, show me the step. When fear hurries my feet, slow them. Give me a hand to hold, and the grace to take it. Let the doubts settle in the dark, and let me wake on firmer ground.
What do you do at a door you are afraid will stay shut, and with a burden that does not come off?
The passage

paras.t: He knocked, therefore, more than once or twice, saying-- "May I now enter here? Will he within Open to sorry me, though I have been An undeserving rebel? Then shall I Not fail to sing his lasting praise on high." At last there came a grave person to the gate, named Good-will, who asked who was there? and whence he came? and what he would have? … CHR. Here is a poor burdened sinner. I come from the City of Destruction, but am going to Mount Zion, that I may be delivered from the wrath to come. I would therefore, Sir, since I am informed that by this gate is the way thither, know if you are willing to let me in? GOOD-WILL. I am willing with all my heart, said he; and with that he opened the gate. … Then I saw in my dream that Christian asked him further if he could not help him off with his burden that was upon his back; for as yet he had not got rid thereof, nor could he by any means get it off without help. He told him, As to thy burden, be content to bear it, until thou comest to the place of deliverance; for there it will fall from thy back of itself.

spans.t: Reflection

Every long day ends at a door. A heavy wooden one, perhaps, with a bell you are not sure you may ring, in a village you have never seen, with a pack that has become part of your body. You have been looking forward to it for hours, and now that you are in front of it, a small hesitation arrives. What if it is full? What if they ask something you cannot answer? What if you are simply in the wrong place?

Christian has the same hesitation on a larger scale. Earlier he was told to head for a little gate at the end of a field, and now he has got there, scratched and muddy, after a bog and a wrong turning we are not reading. He knocks, and nothing happens. So he knocks again,
more than once or twice
, and he says, in a few lines of verse, what he fears: will the person inside open to a
sorry
man, who has been an
undeserving rebel
? Notice that he does not argue his case. He asks. It is the voice of someone who has decided he must try anyway, though he expects to be refused.

The door opens. A grave person called Good-will asks who is there, and whence he came, and what he would have. Christian's answer is the plainest thing in the passage: a poor burdened sinner, come from the City of Destruction, on his way to Mount Zion, and would you be willing to let him in?
I am willing with all my heart
, says Good-will, and opens the gate. There is no test, no catechism, no waiting in the rain. The only thing Christian has to do is knock and say who he is.

Just outside the passage, Good-will gives him a pull as he steps in. A castle stands near, and its captain shoots arrows at people who come up to the gate. Bunyan's world has enemies in it. Ours may only have a stretch of busy road before the village. Either way the sense is the same: when the door opens, go through it.
Now the part that stays with you. Christian asks the one thing every reader would ask. Can the burden come off here? The answer is not what he hoped.
Be content to bear it
, says Good-will,
until thou comest to the place of deliverance

, and there it will fall from his back of itself. It is a hard thing to be told, at the end of a hard stretch, by someone who has just let you in. But it is also honest. Arriving does not end the carrying. It gives you a direction, a welcome and a place to start from. The hostel door opens, and next morning you lift the pack again.
After the gate, Good-will sends Christian on to the house of a guide called the Interpreter, who has promised to show him
excellent things

. We do not have room for all of the rooms. The one that fits this morning best is a little parlour with two children in it, named Passion and Patience. Passion is cross, because he has been told to wait for his best things until next year, and he wants all of them now. He is given a bag of treasure and spends it all, and is left with rags. Patience sits quietly, and, the Interpreter says, will be the one to laugh last. It is a small sketch, but it is a fair picture of what a long walk teaches. You cannot have the whole road this afternoon. Nobody can walk the ~240 km of this road in a day, and anyone who tries to go faster than the road allows may end up, like Passion, with nothing in hand.
There are other rooms in the Interpreter's house that are much darker, and the About chapter says what they are and why we leave them out. This morning only the one parlour is open.

A word of doubt, to keep this honest. A real door on a real road is sometimes locked, or full, or shut for the afternoon, and no one inside is willing with all their heart. Bunyan's gate is not a promise about hostels. If the first door does not open, you ask at the next. What the passage gives you is a habit, and the habit is to knock, and to say plainly who you are and what you need. It is more use than a plan.
For the walk

items.t: Which door am I standing outside today, and what am I waiting to be invited to do?
Be the first to say hello. At every person you pass, a walker, a farmer, someone at a window, give the greeting first:
bom caminho
in Portuguese,
Buen Camino
in Spanish. It costs nothing, and it is a small way of knocking. Then notice what the greeting does to your own shoulders.

spans.t: At the end of the day

By this third evening you have a routine, or the beginnings of one: where the shoes go, which pocket holds the pen, what you wash first. Routines are quiet things, and they are one of the kindnesses of a road. A walk that has settled into one has begun to hold you up.

Count the doors you passed through today. Some were actual doors: a café, a church, a hostel, a shop where you asked for water. Others were doors of another kind, a conversation you began or did not, a question you put to a stranger, a moment when you could have said
I am a bit lost
and said
I am fine
instead. How did each of them feel, going up to it? How did each feel on the other side?

Bunyan's gate asks nothing difficult. It asks only that the man knock, and say who he is. That may be harder than it sounds. Most of us would rather arrive having already earned a welcome, and it is easier to be admired than to be let in. If you spent today wanting to arrive without having asked anything of anyone, that is very human, and a road is a good place to practise the other thing.
And then the burden, which did not fall. Perhaps you felt it again today, a little lighter than yesterday or a little heavier.
Be content to bear it

is a strange instruction, and it sounds like resignation. Read another way, it sounds more like permission: you do not have to be rid of it by tonight, and nobody is keeping score. The pack is a thing you put down at the end of the day and pick up in the morning, and so, for now, is the other weight.

A word for Patience, too. If you were in a hurry today, to cover more than you planned, to reach the next place sooner, to feel the benefit of the walk before it was ready, you were Passion for an afternoon. Nothing bad has happened. Patience is simply the habit of making the best things last, and a long road is generous with chances to practise it.

If the last stretch to your door today was along a road, let it be a small reminder to take that part slowly. Where there is no verge, walkers are usually advised to keep to the side facing the oncoming traffic, and to step well off the road when a vehicle passes. Bunyan's gate has arrows near it, and the last approach to a welcome is a place where people hurry and forget to look.

It is also worth noticing what was waiting on the other side. A stamp in a pilgrim's passport, a plate of something hot, a bunk with a number on it, a stranger's nod: none of it was earned in any sense that a ledger would recognise, and all of it was a gift. That is a good thing to say thank you for, to someone or to nobody.

items.t: What door did I hesitate at today, and what happened when I went through it?
Where did I want to be rid of something that has to be carried a while longer?
Was there an hour today when I wanted everything at once?

spans.t: A short prayer

Give me the courage to knock, and the plainness to say who I am. Let me be content to carry what I must until the carrying is done. Teach me the patience of someone who can wait for the best things. Open the door tonight, and let me sleep inside it.

chapters.title: Day 4. The arbour on the hill

spans.t: How do you climb, and where do you let yourself rest?
The passage

paras.t: He ran thus till he came at a place somewhat ascending, and upon that place stood a cross, and a little below, in the bottom, a sepulchre. So I saw in my dream, that just as Christian came up with the cross, his burden loosed from off his shoulders, and fell from off his back, and began to tumble, and so continued to do, till it came to the mouth of the sepulchre, where it fell in, and I saw it no more. … I looked, then, after Christian, to see him go up the hill, where I perceived he fell from running to going, and from going to clambering upon his hands and his knees, because of the steepness of the place. Now, about the midway to the top of the hill was a pleasant arbour, made by the Lord of the hill for the refreshing of weary travellers; thither, therefore, Christian got, where also he sat down to rest him.

cite.t: , Part One, the Cross and the Hill Difficulty (English original, 1678)

spans.t: Reflection

There is a gradient at which conversation stops. You know it when you reach it: the sentences get shorter, then a single word, then only breathing and the sound of boots. Somebody ahead of you has their hands on their knees, and you do not need to ask why.

The passage has two halves, and they are very different in weight. The first is the heart of Bunyan's story. Christian, still bent under the burden, comes to a rising piece of ground, and on it stands a cross, and a little below it a sepulchre, which is an old word for a tomb. As he comes up to the cross, the burden loosens from his shoulders and falls from his back, tumbling until it drops into the mouth of the tomb, and he sees it no more. In the lines that follow, he gives three leaps for joy and goes on singing. Three shining beings tell him his sins are forgiven, strip off his rags and dress him in clean clothes, set a mark on his forehead and give him a roll with a seal on it to carry. This is a Christian image, and for Bunyan the centre of everything. We say so plainly. A reader who does not share the faith can still see the shape, and the shape is this: the weight comes off at a place, not as a prize for effort, and not before the story says so. Christian did not shrug it off. It fell.

You may recognise something in that, whatever you call it: a grief that eased on an ordinary afternoon without being asked, or a decision that stopped hurting. It does not come by timetable, and Bunyan is careful about that. It took Christian a bog, a gate and a good deal of running to get here. Most days nothing of the sort happens, and the burden is still on your back when you wake. Some days it does not.

The second half of the passage is about the very next thing, and it is a hill. Bunyan calls it the Hill Difficulty, and the narrow way goes straight up it. Notice how he describes the climb: Christian
fell from running to going, and from going to clambering upon his hands and his knees

. There are three gears, and he goes through all of them, and Bunyan does not say a word against him for it. Anyone who has gone up a long hill in the heat knows that sequence. The man who ran at the cross is on his hands and knees by the top, and nothing in the book suggests he has done anything wrong.
Halfway up, he finds a pleasant arbour, a shaded seat that the
Lord of the hill

has put there for the refreshing of weary travellers. Someone thought of you. Someone built a seat, in a shady place, at exactly the point where a walker would want one. A bench by a path, a fountain in a square, a shelter with a roof and a wall, a tap at a churchyard gate: none of them is yours, and all of them are meant for whoever comes. Christian sits down to rest, and the passage stops there.

The story does not. He falls asleep, and his roll slips out of his hand. He walks on without it, and only at the top does he feel for it and find it gone, and then he has to go all the way back to the arbour to look for it, scolding himself at every step. Bunyan is severe about this: the arbour, he says, was only meant for
a little refreshment for his weariness

. We think he is too hard on the man. A rest is part of climbing, and a sleep in the shade is not a sin. But the practical sense in the story is right, and it is easy to take. Before you leave a place where you have rested, touch your pockets.
A pilgrim's nearest thing to the roll is the
credencial
, the folded card that walkers carry and have stamped along the way (a stamp is a
sello
in Spanish, a
carimbo

in Portuguese). We are not saying that Bunyan's roll is a credencial, and it is not the same thing. We only mean that there is something you cannot do without, and a bench is the very place you may leave it.

One caution, in plain words. If a climb brings chest pain, faintness or confusion, that is not the time for Bunyan's three gears. Stop, sit in the shade, drink, and ask someone for help. In Spain and Portugal the emergency number is 112.
For the walk

items.t: Which gear am I in right now, and is it the right one for this hill?

When you next sit down, whether it is a bench, a wall or a kerb, stay long enough to drink some water and look at the view. Then, before you stand up, touch each pocket and the top of your pack once, and say aloud what is in it. It takes ten seconds, and it is worth it.

spans.t: At the end of the day

If there was no hill today, there was something that felt like one: a long, straight afternoon, a stretch of tarmac, an argument that would not leave your head. The gears were the same. Think about which one you were in for most of the day, and whether you chose it or only found yourself there.

Running, going, clambering. If you want a rule for tomorrow's hill, go at a pace at which you could still say a short sentence aloud, and drop a gear before you have to. Most days you will go through all three, and it is easy to forget that the order does not matter. A day that began at a run can end on hands and knees, and the other way round. None of it tells you anything about the road, or about you, except what your legs know. Bunyan does not shame his man for the crawl. It is worth the same courtesy tonight.

Then the arbour. Where did you stop today, and what did the stopping give you? A rest that leaves you more tired than before is not a rest, and a rest that lasts too long can cost an afternoon, as Christian found. Both are easy mistakes, and the cure for both is only to notice. Did the bench do its work? Did you thank whoever put it there, in your head or aloud? Someone also put out the water, mended the path, painted the arrow, and kept the church open so that you could sit in the cool. Most of the kindness of a road is done by people you will never meet.

And did the burden shift at all? It may have, and if so, take the lightness as it comes and do not examine it. It may not, and then Day 3 still holds: be content to bear it a while longer. The cross in the story stands at a particular place, and nobody gets there by trying harder.

Tonight, unlike Christian, you are allowed to sleep, and to sleep soundly. A day of hills leaves the body glad of any chair, and an evening is a poor time for hard thinking. The questions below will keep.

Last of all, the pockets. It is the most ordinary thing in the whole reading, and the one most likely to matter tomorrow. Count what you came with: the pass, the phone, the wallet, the hat. If you carry a credencial, take it out and look at today's stamp, with its place and its date and its slightly smudged ink. It is a small proof that you were here, and the kind of thing that is easy to lose and hard to replace. If something is missing tonight, it is better to know now, while the place where you may have left it is still open.

items.t: Which gear was I in for most of today, and did I choose it?
Where did I rest, and did the rest give back what it took?
Did I leave anything behind today, on a bench or in a café, that I should go back for, or let go?

spans.t: A short prayer
For the hill, give me breath. For the bench, give me thanks. If my burden slips from me, let me notice. If it does not, let me carry it well. Let me wake in the morning with everything I came with.
Who asks you where you have come from, and what does it do to be asked kindly?
The passage

paras.t: Then she asked him whence he was, and whither he was going, and he told her. She asked him also how he got into the way; and he told her. Then she asked him what he had seen and met with in the way; and he told her. … So she smiled, but the water stood in her eyes; and after a little pause, she said, I will call forth two or three more of the family. So she ran to the door, and called out Prudence, Piety, and Charity, who, after a little more discourse with him, had him into the family; and many of them, meeting him at the threshold of the house, said, Come in, thou blessed of the Lord; this house was built by the Lord of the hill, on purpose to entertain such pilgrims in. Then he bowed his head, and followed them into the house. … Thus they discoursed together till late at night; and after they had committed themselves to their Lord for protection, they betook themselves to rest: the Pilgrim they laid in a large upper chamber, whose window opened towards the sun-rising: the name of the chamber was Peace; where he slept till break of day, and then he awoke and sang-- "Where am I now? Is this the love and care Of Jesus for the men that pilgrims are? Thus to provide! that I should be forgiven! And dwell already the next door to heaven!"

cite.t: , Part One, the Palace Beautiful (English original, 1678)

spans.t: Reflection

At the end of a long day the first questions are always the same. Where did you start this morning? How far have you come? Where are you heading tomorrow? They are asked at doors, over soup, across a bunk, and they are asked so often that they can sound like a form to be filled in. Then, now and then, someone asks them as if the answer mattered.

Christian reaches such a place at nightfall, after the hill and the arbour, and after the worst fright of the day. Bunyan sets two lions in the narrow way up to the house, and Christian sees them and stops, and thinks of going back. Then comes a line that is worth keeping:
The lions were chained, but he saw not the chains.

The porter, whose name is Watchful, calls out that they are chained, and that he should keep to the middle of the path. They roar, and do him no harm. It is a very small piece of wisdom for a walker with an active imagination. Some of what frightens you on the way is chained, and you cannot see the chain from where you stand.

At the door a grave young woman called Discretion, who is one of the household, comes out and asks him who he is. The passage gives it in a rhythm that is almost a lullaby. She asks whence he came and whither he is going, and he tells her. She asks how he got into the way, and he tells her. She asks what he has seen and met with on it, and he tells her. Three times Bunyan writes the same plain clause,
and he told her
, and you can feel the story being drawn out of a tired man a piece at a time, and being heard.

Then comes the detail that makes the scene. She smiles, but the water stands in her eyes. She is moved by what he has said. She goes to fetch the rest of the family, and they meet him on the threshold with a welcome:
Come in, thou blessed of the Lord
. This house, they say, was built for such pilgrims as he. He bows his head and follows them in.

Think what that does to a person. To be asked about your road by someone who has time for the answer, and to see it land, is a rare form of rest. It may be more than the bed. Most of us carry the story of the day undelivered, and a good host, or a good friend, or a stranger across a table, is a person to whom it can be delivered. You do not have to make it good. Three sentences will do. The listener does the rest.
There is a second half to the passage, and it is the quietest. They give Christian a large upper room, with a window that opens towards the sunrise, and its name is
Peace
. He sleeps until the day breaks, wakes, and sings, and the song is a kind of astonishment:
Where am I now?
he asks, and cannot believe that he is provided for, that he is forgiven, and that he lives
already the next door to heaven
. It is not a deep thought. It is the plain pleasure of a good bed after a hard day, with morning at the window.

Now the honest part. The house is generous, and it is also a little stern. After the welcome, its members question him closely before supper, even about the family he left behind. He is kept for a few days. They show him the records of the house and then an armoury, and before he goes they dress him from head to foot in armour, because a bad stretch is waiting for him just beyond the next hill. In Bunyan's story, rest is also preparation. And a reader who has not come for any of this should not feel they owe a host an inner life along with the fee. A bunk, a soup and a quiet corner can be hospitality enough.

Bunyan also gives his house a name, the Palace Beautiful, and four women to keep it: Discretion, Prudence, Piety and Charity. They are the virtues of a good host. Perhaps they are the virtues of a good guest as well: to arrive without fuss, to take your turn, and to be glad of what is on the table.
For the walk

items.t: Who has asked me where I started, and have I let them hear the whole answer?

Today, instead of asking the next walker you meet which country they come from, ask where they started this morning, or where they began the whole road. Then listen to everything they say, without finishing their sentences. When it is your turn, tell yours in three sentences, and stop. Notice how much you want to say, and how little is needed.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Wherever you are sleeping tonight, whether it is a single room, a bunk among twenty, or a floor with a mat on it, the room has a name of its own, and you may not have thought to ask it. Bunyan calls his
Peace
, and he calls it that before anyone has slept in it, as a wish. Name tonight's room for what you hope it will hold.

Peace in a shared room is not guaranteed. Someone will snore, someone will rustle a bag at dawn, someone will shine a torch in your eyes. It is part of what a pilgrim's house costs, and it is a small thing next to what it gives. A courtesy goes a long way in a dormitory: pack the night before, keep the light low, and say good morning to whoever you wake. You are somebody else's noise tonight.

Go back over the day and listen for the stories. Whose did you hear? It need not have been long: where someone planned to stop, why someone had come, whom someone was missing at home. The best listening is the kind that is not interrupted, even when you have a better story to tell. And whose story did you hold back? Some stories wait until the evening, and for some there is no good listener on the road.

The lions, too. What frightened you today, and what turned out to be chained? A road is full of things that look worse from a distance: a dog behind a gate, a stretch of traffic, a hill on the map, a conversation you were afraid to have. Perhaps you passed one without trouble and only realised afterwards that it had not been loose at all. That is worth knowing for tomorrow.

Try telling the day in three sentences, as Christian told his story at the door: where I started, what I met on the way, where I am bound. You may be surprised how much of a day fits into them, and how much of it you can then put down. If nobody is there to hear it, say it quietly to yourself, or write it in a notebook, or send it to someone who would like to know.

It is true that the evening is the loneliest part of the day for many people who walk alone. If tonight is like that, a message home counts as a listener, and so does a bowl of soup at a table where someone else is eating. Nobody asks for a performance.

Be gentle about the end of a long day. If you arrived too tired to listen, or to tell, or to be anyone's company, that is not a failure. A bed, and a quiet room, and a morning at the window are enough for one night.

items.t: Whose story did I listen to today, and did I stay to hear the end?
What did I fear today that turned out to be chained?
What would I call the room I am sleeping in tonight?

spans.t: A short prayer
For the roof, the bread and the bed, my thanks. Bless whoever opened the door tonight, and whoever will rise early to close it. Let this be a room called Peace. Let its window face the morning.
What do you say when the voice you dread reads out your faults, and every item is accurate?
The passage

paras.t: APOL. Thou didst faint at first setting out, when thou wast almost choked in the Gulf of Despond; thou didst attempt wrong ways to be rid of thy burden, whereas thou shouldst have stayed till thy Prince had taken it off; thou didst sinfully sleep and lose thy choice thing; thou wast, also, almost persuaded to go back at the sight of the lions; and when thou talkest of thy journey, and of what thou hast heard and seen, thou art inwardly desirous of vain-glory in all that thou sayest or doest. CHR. All this is true, and much more which thou hast left out; but the Prince whom I serve and honour is merciful, and ready to forgive; but, besides, these infirmities possessed me in thy country, for there I sucked them in; and I have groaned under them, been sorry for them, and have obtained pardon of my Prince.

cite.t: , Part One, the Valley of Humiliation (English original, 1678)

spans.t: Reflection

Downhill is not the easy half of a walk. Anyone whose knees have taken a long descent knows it: each step lands a little harder than the one before, the toes press into the front of the boot, and a loose stone is a real danger. Bunyan knew it too. When the household at the Palace Beautiful walk Christian down to the valley, he goes down
very warily
, and still
caught a slip or two
. His hosts give him a loaf of bread, a bottle of wine and a cluster of raisins before they leave him, and that is the right provision for a downhill stretch.

The valley has a name that sounds like a punishment, the Valley of Humiliation. It is only low ground. Humility and humus, the Latin word for earth, share a root, and the valley is simply the place nearest the ground. But Bunyan's low ground is not quiet. Almost at once a monster comes over the field to meet Christian. He has scales like a fish, wings like a dragon, feet like a bear, fire and smoke from his belly, and a mouth like a lion's. His name is Apollyon. Christian thinks about turning back, and then remembers that he has no armour for his back, so he stands his ground.

What the monster does first is not fight. He talks. He claims Christian as his subject, he urges him to come home, he offers him better wages, and he says that servants of the other master tend to come to a bad end. When none of that works he does the cleverest thing a critic can do, and reads Christian his own record. That is the passage.

Look at the list. It is not made up. Christian fainted at the beginning, when he was almost choked in the bog, which Apollyon calls by a slightly different name. He tried wrong ways to be rid of his burden, a detour we did not read. He slept when he should not have, and lost the roll that was his pass. He was nearly talked into going back at the sight of the lions. And when he talks about his journey, says the monster, he is secretly after praise. Three of those five are things this book has already shown you, one at a time, in these pages: the bog, the sleep, the lions. The accuser has been keeping notes.
Now notice what Christian does. He does not argue. He does not say that the bog was not his fault, or that anybody would have slept, or that the lions were frightening. He says:
All this is true, and much more which thou hast left out

. That is a remarkable sentence. He confesses the list and adds to it. He is more honest about himself than his accuser. And in the same breath he goes on: the Prince he serves is merciful and ready to forgive, these weaknesses were already in him when he left his old country, and he has been sorry for them and has been pardoned.

There is the pattern of the day. A voice reads out your faults, and it is accurate, and the test is what you do with the accuracy. The accuser wants it to be a reason to turn round. Christian takes it as a plain account, says
that is true
, and carries on walking. Humility of that sort is not self-contempt. It is accuracy about yourself, held without panic.

Two hard things need saying. First, the story is a fight with a devil, and the fight takes more than half a day and leaves Christian wounded and nearly beaten before it is done. Some readers will put a name like the inner critic, or the voice at three in the morning, in place of Apollyon. The passage works either way, and we need not choose for you. Second, the answer
all this is true

does not fit every accusation. Some are unfair, and some are exaggerated, and some come from people with their own reasons. If the voice is saying that you are worthless, that is not true, and it is not a list at all. And where the true thing is that you hurt someone, humility asks for more than a sigh. It asks you to put it right.

In an ordinary day it asks something small. Notice what the critic says on the descent, on the mile you are walking slowest, on the day somebody passes you. Ask which part is simply the case. A slow pace, a wrong turn, a sharp word at breakfast: say that it is true, and then take the next step. Humility is a good companion on a downhill, because it keeps your eyes on your feet.
For the walk

items.t: If the voice in my head read out today's faults, which would be simply true?
Choose one small true fault, perhaps your pace, a wrong turning or a grumble, and say to yourself, quietly,
that is true
. Then walk ten steps without arguing with it or adding to it. On the tenth step, add one plain sentence of your own:
and I am still walking
. See whether it changes the weight.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Before any questions, a plain thing. Have you eaten? Christian is given bread, wine and raisins before he meets the monster, and not after. A critic is much louder on an empty stomach, and most accusations sound less final once there is soup in the body. If the voice was hard on you today, look at your supper before you look at your soul.

Then go back to the descent, whichever it was. A real one, with sore knees, or a figurative one: a mistake, a mood, a conversation that went lower than you wanted. What was the critic's version of the day? Try to put it into three or four sentences, in its own words, harsh and complete. That may be harder than it sounds, because we are used to hearing it as a noise and not as a text.

Then do what Christian does. Go through the sentences, one at a time, and mark the ones that are true. You will probably find some. Say so, plainly, without defending. And then notice what the critic left out. It left out the miles. It left out the hour you sat with someone else's trouble, the water you gave, the moment you took the correct turning after hesitating. Christian says his accuser has left out
much more
, and he means the faults. You may find that the accuser has left out much more of the other kind too. A list that is accurate only in one direction is not an account.

There is a line in the fight itself that is worth taking to bed. At the worst of it Christian is flat on the ground, and his sword has flown out of his hand. He reaches for it and catches it, and says
when I fall I shall arise
. He does not say that he will not fall. He has just fallen. The sentence is about what happens after.

If one of the true items on tonight's list was about another person, something said sharply or something left undone, then put it where you can find it tomorrow. A short message, a word at breakfast, a small amends. It does not have to be large, and it does not have to be done tonight. It only has to be done.
It is also all right to find that none of it is true. Some days the voice is wrong, and then the honest thing is to say that, and to go to bed.
And be easy on your legs. A day of descent is hard on the knees and calves, and the night is the time they send their reply. Water, a stretch, a seat with the feet up, and bed.

items.t: What did the critic in my head say today, and which part was simply true?
What did it leave out?
Have I eaten and drunk enough to hear it fairly?

spans.t: A short prayer

Let me be honest about what I am, and kind about what I am not. When my faults are read to me, let me say that is true and keep walking. Feed me before the fight. Teach me to go downhill with care, and to be at home on low ground.
Who else is on this stretch with you, and may be thinking they are alone?
The passage

paras.t: The pathway was here also exceeding narrow, and therefore good Christian was the more put to it; for when he sought, in the dark, to shun the ditch on the one hand, he was ready to tip over into the mire on the other; also when he sought to escape the mire, without great carefulness he would be ready to fall into the ditch. Thus he went on, and I heard him here sigh bitterly; for, besides the dangers mentioned above, the pathway was here so dark, and ofttimes, when he lift up his foot to set forward, he knew not where or upon what he should set it next. … When Christian had travelled in this disconsolate condition some considerable time, he thought he heard the voice of a man, as going before him, saying, "Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for thou art with me." … Then he was glad, and that for these reasons: First, Because he gathered from thence, that some who feared God were in this valley as well as himself.

cite.t: , Part One, the Valley of the Shadow of Death (English original, 1678)

spans.t: Reflection

Every walk has its grey hours. The light goes flat, the path is the same in every direction, and nothing you can point to has gone wrong. Or something has gone wrong, and you cannot see how to mend it, and the next step is a matter of faith in the ground. Such hours do not need a night to happen in, although a night will do.

Bunyan gives them a place, the Valley of the Shadow of Death, and it is the darkest page of his road. The narrow way runs between a deep ditch on one hand and a dangerous bog on the other. The ditch, he says, is where the blind have led the blind. The bog is a quag with no bottom, and even a good man who falls into it cannot find a place to put his foot.

That is the first half of the passage, and its sharpest line is about steering. When Christian tries to keep clear of the ditch, he is ready to tip over into the mire. When he tries to keep clear of the mire, he is ready to fall into the ditch. Most people know that dance in some form. You push too hard because you fear being late, and then you fear the pain and stop. You try to be cheerful after a gloomy morning, and cannot keep it up. You swing from one danger to the other, and the path between them is only as wide as your foot. It is dark besides, and when he lifts his foot to move forward,
he knew not where or upon what he should set it next
. Few sentences say it so well: you do not know what the next step will land on, and you take it.

The second half is a small miracle. In the dark, some way along, Christian thinks he hears a man's voice ahead of him. It is saying words that he knows, from the twenty-third Psalm: though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for thou art with me. And Christian is glad, and he gives his reasons. The first is the one the passage keeps: some who feared God are in this valley as well as himself. He is not the only one. Someone has gone ahead of him, in the same dark, saying the same words.
A little later he calls out to the man in front, and gets no answer. Bunyan explains why: the man in front
also thought to be alone

. Hold that one for a minute. The voice ahead of you thought it was alone. Whoever is a few hundred metres up the path, in the same weather, with the same ache, may think so too, and may not have heard you, and may not know you are there. Not every call is answered. But hearing someone was enough to change the valley, and in a little while the day broke, and Christian said that God had turned
the shadow of death into the morning
The detail that comes next is as true as any in the book. In the daylight, Christian looks back,
not out of desire to return, but to see

what he had come through in the dark. He sees how narrow the way was between the ditch and the mire. It is hard to look back at a bad stretch with any other purpose than wishing it away. To look at it in good light, simply to know what it was, is another thing, and it is a form of courage.

Three honest remarks. First, this valley is full of terrors that the passage leaves out, fiends and flames and a mouth of hell beside the path, and the book says Christian was worse put to it here than in his fight with Apollyon. Among them are blasphemous thoughts whispered in his ear, which he took for his own. If thoughts come to you that you did not choose and cannot shake, and they are heavy or last for days, talk to a doctor or someone you trust. Asking for that kind of help is no weakness. It is the same thing as calling out to the voice ahead. Second, at the far end of the valley the book turns to a quarrel of Bunyan's century, and the About chapter says what we left out. Third, a plain safety word. An actual road in the dark is not a place for proving anything. Start in daylight, and if dusk catches you, stop at the next place with a roof and a light. In an emergency the number in Spain and Portugal is 112.
For the walk

items.t: Who else is on this stretch of the road, ahead of me or behind, who may think they are alone?

In the quiet part of the walk, say one line aloud that you would like someone behind you to hear: a greeting, a verse, the last words of a song. It need not be anything solemn. A voice ahead may be the only company somebody has this hour. If you hear one ahead of you, notice whether it helps.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The grey hour of the day has probably passed by now, whatever it was. Go back to where it began. It may have been a long road beside a field with no end, or the mid-afternoon dip, or a moment of fear that came from nowhere. Perhaps there was a moment when two possible mistakes stood on either side, and any step looked wrong.

In the story, Christian's path is narrow between the ditch and the mire. What were your two? Starting too fast against stopping too early, perhaps. Pressing on against giving in. Telling someone how you felt against saying that you were fine. Most of us have a favourite ditch. It helps to know which one it is, because that is the one we fall into when we are afraid.

Then look at that stretch once more, in the light of evening, as Christian does at dawn: not out of desire to return, but to see what it was. It is often smaller than it felt when you were inside it. It is sometimes exactly as narrow as it felt, and then it is something you have come through, and you can say so.

Think now about the voices ahead. Was there one today? It might have been a laugh at a café, a language you could not follow in a tone you understood, a pair of boots you saw far up a path, a message that arrived from home when it was needed. And whose voice might you have been for someone behind you? You may never know. A greeting, said without thought, can be the one thing someone hears that day.

There is a careful point in the second half of the Valley, beyond the passage. When the sun comes up, Bunyan says that the rest of the way is, if anything, more dangerous than the first half, so full of traps and pits that Christian could not have crossed it in the dark. But he can see them now. It is a useful thing to know. Many hard things can be faced in daylight that cannot be faced at night.

One small job for tonight. If tomorrow's start is before sunrise, a head torch is worth having, and worth checking tonight while there is still a light to check it by. Do not set out into an unfamiliar dark on a bad road if you can wait for the dawn.

If tonight is low, be plain about it. Tiredness paints everything grey. Eat something, wash, lie down, and take no large decision before morning. If the low feeling is more than tiredness, and does not lift, or grows, tell someone: the host, a friend, a doctor. If you are in danger, the number is 112.

items.t: When did the path narrow today, and which two dangers was I swinging between?
Whose voice did I hear ahead of me, and whose might have heard mine?
What looks different tonight, in the evening light, from how it looked this afternoon?

spans.t: A short prayer

In the dark stretches, let me hear a voice ahead of me. Let me be one for someone behind. Show me where to set my foot, and if I cannot see, let me stand still until the light. Turn the shadow into morning.
What do you actually want from today?
The passage

paras.t: And as they wondered at their apparel, so they did likewise at their speech; for few could understand what they said; they naturally spoke the language of Canaan, but they that kept the fair were the men of this world; so that, from one end of the fair to the other, they seemed barbarians each to the other. … But that which did not a little amuse the merchandisers was, that these pilgrims set very light by all their wares; they cared not so much as to look upon them; and if they called upon them to buy, they would put their fingers in their ears, and cry, Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity, and look upwards, signifying that their trade and traffic was in heaven. … One chanced mockingly, beholding the carriage of the men, to say unto them, What will ye buy? But they, looking gravely upon him, answered, "We buy the truth."

spans.t: Reflection

The road passes through towns, and towns sell things. There are bakeries, cafés, a pharmacy where you can ask for a plaster, a stall with shells on strings, a shop whose window is full of every kind of walking stick. A pilgrim on foot is in the market whether or not they mean to be. You are carrying money, you are hungry, and you are new.

Bunyan has a town of his own for this, and a fair in it that never closes. It is called Vanity, and the fair is Vanity Fair. Before the pilgrims arrive, Bunyan lists what is sold there, and it is a long list: houses and lands, honours and titles, pleasures of every kind, and in the end lives and souls. It is a picture of a world in which everything has a price, and the pilgrims have to pass through it because the road to the city goes straight through the town.

Take care with this one. Bunyan's fair is not the café where you will have lunch, and it is not a verdict on the people who sell bread and postcards to walkers. A village is a home, and many of the people who live on a pilgrim road keep the Way going. Nothing here should make you look down on a stall-holder. It is a satire, and it is aimed at a particular kind of greed, and the pilgrims in it are hardly models of manners. What Bunyan has caught is how it feels to be a stranger who is passing through.
First, you are different. The pilgrims' clothes are unlike those of anyone who trades in the fair, and the whole town stares. Then comes a line that any foreign walker will understand:
few could understand what they said

. Bunyan has them speak the language of Canaan, which is his way of saying that they talk like people from another country, and the town and the pilgrims seem like barbarians to each other. You may know a small version of this: a conversation in which both sides are friendly and neither follows. The boots, the pack, the sunburn and the shell make you a visible stranger. That can be a kind of freedom, and it can be a weight.
One sentence from a stretch we have not quoted is worth keeping. Anyone who wants to go to the city and yet not go through this town, Bunyan says,
must needs go out of the world
. There is no road round it. A pilgrimage is not a way of avoiding money, shops and people with something to sell. It goes through them, and the question is how you walk.
Second, they do not look at the wares. When the sellers call to them to buy, the pilgrims put their fingers in their ears, and cry
Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity, and look upwards
. And then comes the best question in the passage. Someone says, half in mockery,
What will ye buy?
And the pilgrims look gravely at him and answer:
We buy the truth.
Nobody would recommend that answer to a stall-holder. A stall-holder who asks what you will buy is only doing a job, and the polite reply is
a coffee, please
or
just looking, thank you

. But as a question put to your whole day, it is very good. What are you buying with this walk? Not with the euros in your pocket: with the hours. You may not have a noble answer. Time, a quiet head, a body that works again, a stamp in a book, a long talk, an end to a bad year. Some answers are only a way of saying that you need to be somewhere else for a while. All of them are fair, and it is useful to know which one is yours.

Now the hard part. In the pages after this, the town turns on the pilgrims, and what follows is not a market at all. They are mocked, beaten, put in a cage, and brought before a judge. One of them, Faithful, is condemned and burned at the stake. Bunyan had himself been jailed for what he believed, which may be why these pages are so bitter. We have stopped where it is still only a question, and we do not read on. Nor should you read it as a rule that a pilgrim is always right and a town is always wrong. Real towns are neither.

What it asks of an ordinary day is small. Before you go into a shop or a café, know what you came for. Come out with it. Keep your head up, and let the town go about its own day, which is not yours. And be a good stranger: thank people, in their language if you can, and give a plain answer to a plain question.
For the walk

items.t: What do I actually want from the next hour?
Before you go into a shop or café today, stop at the door and say to yourself, in a few words, what you came in for. Buy that, and say thank you in the local language:
obrigado
if you are a man,
obrigada
if you are a woman, in Portugal, or
gracias
in Spain. Notice what the pause does.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Count up what you bought today. Water, bread, something sweet, a hot drink, a plaster, a postcard. If you are honest the list is probably short, and a few of the things on it were not needed. That is all right. A day is allowed to have a pastry in it. Some of what you bought, you bought because you were tired, or lonely, or bored, and a sweet thing at four o'clock can save a stage. There is nothing to confess. It is only worth knowing which of your purchases were hunger and which were something else.

Then think about what else you spent, because there is another currency, and it is attention. Where did your attention go today? Some of it went where you meant it to go, on the path, on a view, on a person. Some of it went on a screen, or on a thought about the end of the road, or on whatever the next sign was selling. You do not have to be hard on yourself, but it is useful to see where it went, since you have only so much.

Remember where you felt like a stranger. It may have been the way a conversation stopped when you walked into a shop, or a joke you could not follow, or a language you could not read on a menu, or only the sense of being the one person in a square who was going somewhere. What did the strangeness show you? Some people find that it makes them kinder, because they are less sure of themselves. Some find that it makes them stiff. Both are normal. Neither lasts.

Bunyan's pilgrims were not well treated, and the fair thought them mad. You were, we hope, treated much better. Think of the ones who sold you something without fuss, or gave you directions, or only nodded as you went by. A village is a home, and you passed through the middle of somebody's day. A thank-you is the smallest rent there is. If you forgot to give one, there will be another chance tomorrow, and the person at the next counter will be just as glad of it.
It is also worth looking at what cash you have left for tomorrow, since small places on country roads do not always like to take a card, and a long stretch between towns is a poor place to find out.

Last of all, the question. What will ye buy? If you had to answer it for the whole road in a single word, what would the word be? You do not have to say it tonight, and it may change by the weekend. But once it has been said, even silently, you may find that you walk a little differently the next morning.

items.t: What did I actually want today, and did I get it?
Where did I feel like a stranger, and what did it show me?
Whom did I thank today, and in whose language?

spans.t: A short prayer

Let me want what is enough. Let me be a good stranger and a grateful guest. Where I am stared at, let me be gentle. Where I am passed over, let me not turn bitter. Let me spend my attention on what is true.
What do you do when an easier path runs beside the hard one, and what do you carry that you have forgotten?
The passage

paras.t: Now, I beheld in my dream, that they had not journeyed far, but the river and the way for a time parted; at which they were not a little sorry; yet they durst not go out of the way. Now the way from the river was rough, and their feet tender, by reason of their travels; so the souls of the pilgrims were much discouraged because of the way. … Now, a little before them, there was on the left hand of the road a meadow, and a stile to go over into it; and that meadow is called By-path Meadow. Then said Christian to his fellow, If this meadow lieth along by our wayside, let us go over into it. Then he went to the stile to see, and behold, a path lay along by the way, on the other side of the fence. It is according to my wish, said Christian. Here is the easiest going; come, good Hopeful, and let us go over. … Now a little before it was day, good Christian, as one half amazed, brake out in passionate speech: What a fool, quoth he, am I, thus to lie in a stinking Dungeon, when I may as well walk at liberty. I have a Key in my bosom called Promise, that will, I am persuaded, open any Lock in Doubting Castle. Then said Hopeful, That's good news; good Brother pluck it out of thy bosom and try.

cite.t: , Part One, By-path Meadow and Doubting Castle (English original, 1678)

spans.t: Reflection

You know the stretch. The proper way is cobbles, or stones the size of eggs, or hard tarmac that rings in your heels, and beside it, over a low fence or through a gap, runs a strip of soft grass that looks as if it had been laid for tired feet. Nobody would blame you for looking at it.
Bunyan puts exactly that in front of Christian. The river that had kept him company moves away from the way, and the road becomes rough. The pilgrims' feet are
tender, by reason of their travels
, and their spirits sink with them. A little ahead there is a meadow on the left, and a stile to climb over into it. A path runs along the other side of the fence, side by side with the road.
It is according to my wish
, Christian says, and so it is.
Here is the easiest going
Pay attention to Hopeful, the companion who joined Christian after the fair. In the lines the passage skips, he asks the right question:
how if this path should lead us out of the way?

Christian says it does not seem likely, since it runs along the road. And Hopeful, being persuaded, goes over the stile after him. The doubt was spoken, and heard, and then it gave way. It is a common way to go wrong in a pair: one says perhaps, the other says it will be fine, and neither is quite sure.

What follows is Bunyan at his sternest. A man called Vain-confidence, who is walking ahead and says the path goes to the gate, falls into a pit in the dark and is killed. There is thunder and rain, the water rises, and the two cannot get back to the stile. Bunyan's narrator adds a line to himself, in brackets, which is the wisest thing in the episode:
it is easier going out of the way, when we are in, than going in when we are out

. They sleep under a shelter, and in the morning they find that it is in the grounds of Giant Despair, whose castle is called Doubting Castle. He takes them, beats them, and shuts them in a dungeon. They are there from Wednesday morning until Saturday night, with no light, no food and no water.

We say plainly what we have not quoted. On the second day the Giant tells the prisoners that their only way out is to kill themselves, and Christian, in his misery, is half inclined to agree. It is Hopeful who refuses, and what he says is the heart of the whole episode:
let us be patient, and endure a while

. He points out that they have been through worse, that the Giant has fits and may lose the use of his limbs, and that a way out may come. If the thought of ending your life has ever been near you, or comes near on this road, please tell someone today: a doctor, a friend, someone at home, the host where you are staying. If you are in danger now, the emergency number in Spain and Portugal is 112. Despair is a place, and a place can be left.

In the passage, you meet the way out. Before dawn on the Saturday, Christian cries out, as if waking: what a fool he has been, to lie in a stinking dungeon when he could walk free.
