He has a key in his bosom, called Promise, that will open any lock in the castle. He had it all along. Hopeful says it is good news, and tells him to pluck it out and try.

What is the key? In Bunyan's book it is the promises of God, which Christian had stopped thinking of. For you it may be something quite different, and you may be the only one who knows: a reason you set out, a letter, a sentence somebody said once, a plan for a bad day, the plain fact that you have come this far. The thing about the key is that it was in his pocket all the time. The key did not turn every lock with ease, either. One of them, in the lines after the passage, was very stiff, and it opened all the same. Christian and Hopeful had also spent the night praying, which may be the nearest thing a person has to staying awake together and not giving up.

There is one more thing in the story, and it is the kindest. When they first discover that they are lost, Christian says he is sorry, he had led his brother out of the way, and will Hopeful please forgive him. And Hopeful answers:
Be comforted, my brother, for I forgive thee; and believe, too, that this shall be for our good
. When they get out, they set up a pillar at the stile, with a warning cut on it for those who come after.
For the walk

items.t: What easy path runs beside me today, and what does my own small doubt say about it?
At the next junction, fork or tempting shortcut, stop for ten seconds before you step off the way. Look for the waymark, and say Hopeful's question aloud to yourself:
how if this path should lead us out of the way?
Then decide. If you do take the shortcut, take it knowing why.

spans.t: At the end of the day

If the going was rough today, begin with your feet. Take off the socks, look at the soles and between the toes for anything red, wet or tender, and let the skin dry in the air. Tender feet do not get tougher by being ignored.

Most days have a stile in them. It may have been small: a short cut across a car park, a skipped stretch, a bus you did not need to take, a conversation you cut short because it was easier. Some of them are fine. A road with a good alternative is not a sin, and nobody should be made to walk in the wrong shoes for a principle. The question is only whether you asked, as Hopeful did, where the easy path goes.

If you did ask, and went over anyway, notice what it cost, if anything. Bunyan's line says that going out of the way is easier than coming back, and that is a truth about habits as much as about paths. A small stile today can become a large one by the end of the week.

Doubting Castle is a place you may not have visited today, and if so, be glad. But every walker visits it a little, in the form of a long afternoon in which everything looks hopeless and nothing in particular is wrong. If you did, what was in your pocket? It need not be large. It may be a text from someone, or a photograph, or a line you copied on the first day. Take it out now and look at it, because keys are easiest to find in the evening. And if you did spend the afternoon in the castle, and are still there tonight, say so to someone. A bunk in a quiet room is a poor place to keep a giant.

Tiredness is a poor adviser about shortcuts. A day that began with a plan and ended with a bus may have been exactly right, or it may have been the afternoon's fatigue making decisions for the morning. You can tell the difference tomorrow, with a clear head, and meanwhile nothing needs to be settled.

Turn to your companions, too. Did you say something sharp today, to someone you are walking with or beside? Did someone say something to you? Christian and Hopeful began their trouble with an apology and a forgiveness, and it is not hard to believe that this helped them through the days that followed. If there is a sentence waiting to be said tonight, say it.

There is the pillar, too. They did not just escape. They left a sign. It is worth asking what sign you could leave: a word for the next walker about a bad stretch, a note in a visitors' book, a kind word to someone who is a day behind. Much of what you rely on along this road was left by someone who went before.

items.t: When was the easy way tempting today, and what did I ask before I took it?
What do I carry that I have forgotten I have?
Is there someone I should forgive, or ask to forgive me, before I sleep?

spans.t: A short prayer
When the easy way calls, let me ask where it goes. When I am lost, let me forgive and be forgiven quickly. Remind me what is in my pocket. Keep a light for whoever is coming behind.
What can you actually see from here, and what is only something like it?
The passage

paras.t: They went then till they came to the Delectable Mountains, which mountains belong to the Lord of that hill of which we have spoken before; so they went up to the mountains, to behold the gardens and orchards, the vineyards and fountains of water; where also they drank and washed themselves, and did freely eat of the vineyards. Now there were on the tops of these mountains Shepherds feeding their flocks, and they stood by the highway side. The Pilgrims therefore went to them, and leaning upon their staves, (as is common with weary pilgrims when they stand to talk with any by the way), they asked, Whose Delectable Mountains are these? And whose be the sheep that feed upon them? … Then said the Shepherds one to another, Let us here show to the Pilgrims the gates of the Celestial City, if they have skill to look through our perspective glass. The Pilgrims then lovingly accepted the motion; so they had them to the top of a high hill, called Clear, and gave them their glass to look. … Then they essayed to look, but the remembrance of that last thing that the Shepherds had shown them, made their hands shake; by means of which impediment, they could not look steadily through the glass; yet they thought they saw something like the gate, and also some of the glory of the place.

cite.t: , Part One, the Delectable Mountains (English original, 1678)

spans.t: Reflection

Often the best afternoon of a walk comes straight after the worst one. The ground rises, the weather clears, and a place turns up with water in it and a seat in the shade. You have not earned it in any way you could name. It is simply there, and you are a person who has been through something and has come out on the other side of it.

That is what happens to Christian and Hopeful. They get out of Doubting Castle, they put up their warning at the stile, and they walk on until they reach the Delectable Mountains. Bunyan gives them everything a tired person would ask for: gardens and orchards, vineyards and fountains of water. They drink, they wash, and they eat freely. It is one of the places where the book is least afraid of simple pleasure.
On the tops of the mountains are shepherds feeding their flocks, who stand by the road. The pilgrims go up to them,
leaning upon their staves
, and Bunyan adds a parenthesis in the middle of his sentence, which is the loveliest thing in it:
as is common with weary pilgrims when they stand to talk with any by the way

. It is a very old picture, a walker on a stick, resting on it with both hands, talking to someone who lives in the hills. If you walk with poles, you will know the posture. If you do not, you will find that a wall or a gate does as well.

The shepherds' welcome, a few lines on, is the kind you would want. They ask where the pilgrims have come from, and how they got into the way, and then a third question, which is a better one than most hosts ask:
By what means have you so persevered therein?

How did you keep going? Bunyan notes, with a little of his usual sternness, that few who begin the journey ever reach these mountains. When the pilgrims have answered, the shepherds look on them lovingly and say
Welcome to the Delectable Mountains
. They take them to their tents and give them whatever is ready.

Then they show them the city. There is a hill called Clear, a perspective glass, which is an old name for a telescope, and a promise that the gates of the Celestial City can be seen through it. And here is the detail that is rarely noticed. The pilgrims cannot hold the glass steady. Their hands shake. Bunyan says why: it is
the remembrance of that last thing that the Shepherds had shown them
. They manage to see something, and Bunyan is careful about how much.
Yet they thought they saw something like the gate, and also some of the glory of the place

Be clear about what the last thing was, because this is where Bunyan is hardest. Earlier on the same morning the shepherds took the pilgrims to a steep hill where men lay dashed at the bottom, and to a place where blind men wandered among tombs. They said that the blind men had been pilgrims who went over the same stile into the same castle, and were taken, and blinded, and left to wander. Then they opened a door in a hillside, and showed them a by-way to hell. The pilgrims looked at each other with tears running down. That is why the glass shakes.

And that is the true part. Nobody sees clearly with hands that are still shaking from a fright. After a car passes too close, after a dog, after a slip on a wet stone, the body takes a while to settle, and nothing you look at is quite steady. It is not a failure of nerve. You are allowed to wait. And when you do get a glimpse of the thing you were walking towards, it is probably partial: something like the gate, some of the glory. It would be a poor road that showed the whole of it from a hill on the way.

Notice what the shepherds do not do. They do not hurry them. They ask them to stay a while and get acquainted, and they show them things, and they let them look through the glass even though it will not go well. A place that gives you a view you cannot manage, and lets you try, is a generous place.
For the walk

items.t: What can I actually see from here, and what am I trying to see that is not yet in view?

At the first high or open place you come to, stand for a minute leaning on a pole, a wall or a gate. Name three things you can see clearly. Then name one that is hazy, far off or hidden by weather, and do not try to make it clearer. Let your hands be still. That is the whole practice.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The shepherds' question is a good one to carry into the evening: by what means have you so persevered? Not the grand answer. The small ones. What kept you going today, in the dull middle of it? A particular song, a promise of coffee, a pair of boots in front of you, the thought of a person, the plain stubbornness of putting one foot in front of the other. You may find that it is three or four very small things. Say them over once, as the opposite of a list of failings. They are worth knowing, since they are what you will lean on tomorrow.

If your hands, or your voice, shook today after a fright, from a car or a dog or a bad step, that is how a body works. Sit down, drink something, and let it pass. There is nothing to prove, and no view is worth looking at while you are still shaking.

Think, too, about what you saw today and how much of it was only something like. A glimpse of a distant hill, a first sight of a place you had read about, the end of the road turned from an idea into a few days. A view is a good thing, and a view is not a destination. Be glad of what you saw, and do not hold it to account for what it did not show.

If someone who lives here offered you a word today about tomorrow's weather or the next hill, hold on to it. People who live among hills know things that a map cannot show, and Bunyan's shepherds are the ones who know where the ground is bad. A local's word about a river, a path or a sky is worth more than a confident guess.

The shepherds also give the pilgrims whatever is ready, without ceremony. If a hostel or a table offers you a shared meal tonight, take what is put in front of you. It is one of the oldest courtesies of the road, and it is easier to receive than people think.
And then the note. As the pilgrims leave, one of the shepherds gives them
a note of the way

. Later in the story, when they come to a fork where two ways look equally straight, they forget to read it, and are caught in a net. We leave that scene out, but the lesson is plain enough. Read the note when you are at a stand. Tonight, before you sleep, write one for tomorrow: three short lines, where you turn, what you carry, what you remember. Put it in the pocket you will reach for first. It is easier to write a note when you are rested than to find one when you are lost.

items.t: By what means did I keep going today?
What did I see clearly today, and what was only something like?
What will I write on my note for tomorrow's first fork?

spans.t: A short prayer

Let me rest where rest is given. Let the shaking pass from my hands. Show me enough, though it is only something like the whole. Give me a few words on a page to read when I am at a stand. And bless whoever keeps the hills.

chapters.title: Day 11. Two are better than one

spans.t: What keeps you awake, near the end of a long road?
The passage

paras.t: I saw then in my dream, that they went till they came into a certain country, whose air naturally tended to make one drowsy, if he came a stranger into it. And here Hopeful began to be very dull and heavy of sleep; wherefore he said unto Christian, I do now begin to grow so drowsy that I can scarcely hold up mine eyes, let us lie down here and take one nap. CHR. By no means, said the other, lest sleeping, we never awake more. … HOPE. I acknowledge myself in a fault, and had I been here alone I had by sleeping run the danger of death. I see it is true that the wise man saith, Two are better than one. Hitherto hath thy company been my mercy, and thou shalt have a good reward for thy labour. … CHR. Now then, said Christian, to prevent drowsiness in this place, let us fall into good discourse. HOPE. With all my heart, said the other. CHR. Where shall we begin? HOPE. Where God began with us. But do you begin, if you please. CHR. I will sing you first this song:-- When saints do sleepy grow, let them come hither, And hear how these two pilgrims talk together: Yea, let them learn of them, in any wise, Thus to keep ope their drowsy slumb'ring eyes. Saints' fellowship, if it be managed well, Keeps them awake, and that in spite of hell.

cite.t: , Part One, the Enchanted Ground (English original, 1678)

spans.t: Reflection

There is an hour after lunch that every walker knows. The sun is warm, the road is straight, the stomach is full, and the eyelids have begun to weigh something. Nothing is wrong. You are only comfortably, dangerously tired, and a patch of grass by the path looks like the best bed in the world.
Bunyan has a country for that hour, and it comes late in the story, after the mountains, when the end is not far. It is called the Enchanted Ground, and its air
naturally tended to make one drowsy
. Hopeful, who has walked through everything with Christian, says that he can scarcely hold up his eyes, and he suggests that they lie down for one nap. Christian says no, and says why:
lest sleeping, we never awake more
It is worth being fair to Hopeful. In a sentence that is not in the passage, he says that
Sleep is sweet to the labouring man

, and that they might be refreshed by a nap. That is true, and a good deal of walking wisdom agrees with it. A rest in the shade is not a sin, and a body that cannot rest cannot walk. Nobody should take this passage as a rule against sitting down. If it is hot, or you are unwell, or you are simply spent, stop, drink water, and rest in a safe place, not by the edge of a road or a path where you may not be seen.

What Christian is afraid of is narrower and sadder. In Bunyan's story the Enchanted Ground lies near the end of the journey, and the shepherds on the mountains had warned the pilgrims about it. The danger, as we read it, is not tiredness. It is going slack when the end is near: lying down in the middle of the road and not getting up. It is a country where plans can be dropped within sight of the finish.
So what is Christian's remedy? Not a rule, and not a shout. He says,
let us fall into good discourse
. Let us talk. Hopeful agrees with all his heart, and when Christian asks where they should begin, Hopeful gives a good answer:
Where God began with us. But do you begin, if you please

. In other words, tell me how it started. Why did you set out? What was it that made you leave? In the lines that follow, Hopeful tells the whole of his own story, and it is long, and a good deal of it is about doctrine, and we have not quoted it. The point is the question.
How did you come to start this?
is the best question to ask on a drowsy afternoon, and it works as well on a bench in the sun as on any Enchanted Ground.
There is a sentence in the passage that is worth reading again slowly. Hopeful says:
had I been here alone I had by sleeping run the danger of death
. And then:
Hitherto hath thy company been my mercy

. Hopeful is quoting the Bible's book of Ecclesiastes, where the reasoning is plain: two are better than one, because if one falls the other can lift him up. That is as clear a statement of what companionship is for as you will find. It does not say that company is pleasant, although it often is. It says that company has been a mercy, because it kept him awake. And the little song that Christian sings ends with the same idea: fellowship, if it is managed well, keeps people awake.

Two honest things. First, not everyone on this road has a Christian beside them, and some walk alone because they want to. Bunyan is not against solitude. Christian walks alone for long stretches of the book. Later in the same country a young man called Ignorance says that he takes his pleasure in walking alone, and Bunyan means him as a warning. We do not need to follow Bunyan there. A person who walks alone can stay awake in other ways: a phone call to someone at home, a song sung aloud, a podcast, a conversation with a farmer over a wall.

Second, the talk in the book does not stay light. After this passage it becomes long and doctrinal, and sharp, and in the end Christian and Hopeful go on without Ignorance, and the book leaves no doubt which side it is on. You can take the question and leave the rest.
For the walk

items.t: Who is awake with me today, and whom am I helping to stay awake?
When the drowsy hour arrives, ask whoever is beside you how it began:
how did you come to start this?

Then listen. If you are walking alone, ask a friend by message, or say it out loud to yourself, quietly: when did the idea first come, and what was happening then? See whether the answer wakes you up.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The drowsy hour has come and gone. Go back to when it was, and what it felt like. A slow heaviness after a meal, an irritable dullness in the middle of the afternoon, a sudden wish to give up and take a bus. And what woke you? It may have been a hill, or a shout from a car, or someone's voice, or a joke, or the next waymark, or only your own stubbornness. It helps to know what works, because tomorrow it will come again.
A heavy lunch and a hot sun deepen the slump. If today's was a bad one, notice what you ate and how much you drank, and try something lighter and more water tomorrow before you blame your character.

If you walked with a companion today, think of what they gave you without knowing it. Not a great deal, perhaps. A remark about the weather, a pace you could match, a silence that was easy. Hopeful's phrase is
thy company been my mercy
. Is there someone whose company was a mercy to you today? It would be good to tell them, in words, before you sleep. A mercy that is not named tends to go unnoticed.
Notice, too, that the first thing Christian does after proposing talk is to sing. Did you sing today, even under your breath? It is an old and cheap way of keeping the eyes open on a long road.

If you walked alone, what kept you company? A song, a thought, a landscape, a call home? There is no shame in any of it. Some days you need people, and some days you need to be left to yourself, and the road is wide enough for both.

It is also worth saying that the end of a road can be the dangerous part. When it comes within reach, there is a pull to go easy: to cut a corner, to skip the stretching, to stop looking at the waymarks. Feet that have got you this far still need their care, and a map still needs reading, and a bottle still needs filling. A road is not over until you have stopped walking on it.

Plan for tomorrow's slump. If the drowsy hour came at about the same time today as it did yesterday, plan for it. Stop a little before it arrives, in shade, and eat something and drink water, instead of waiting until your head drops. A short, chosen stop is better than a long, forced one.

Last, the opposite of the Enchanted Ground is a proper night. A drowsy afternoon is often the body asking for something you did not give it last night. Tonight, sleep as well as you can: a dark room, a quiet bunk, no screen in your hand. Sleep that is chosen is the best answer to sleep that is simply fallen into.

items.t: When did the drowsy hour come today, and what woke me?
Whose company was a mercy to me today, and have I told them?
If I walked alone, what kept me company?

spans.t: A short prayer

Keep me awake to what matters, and let me sleep soundly when the time comes. Give me a companion for the long afternoons, and let me be one for someone else. Teach me to ask how it began. Do not let the nearness of the end make me careless.
At the last crossing, whose feet are on the ground?
The passage

paras.t: Now, I further saw, that betwixt them and the gate was a river, but there was no bridge to go over: the river was very deep. At the sight, therefore, of this river, the Pilgrims were much stunned; but the men that went in with them said, You must go through, or you cannot come at the gate. … They then addressed themselves to the water and, entering, Christian began to sink, and crying out to his good friend Hopeful, he said, I sink in deep waters; the billows go over my head, all his waves go over me! Selah. … Then said the other, Be of good cheer, my brother, I feel the bottom, and it is good. … Then they both took courage, and the enemy was after that as still as a stone, until they were gone over. Christian therefore presently found ground to stand upon, and so it followed that the rest of the river was but shallow. Thus they got over.

cite.t: , Part One, the River and the gate of the Celestial City (English original, 1678)

spans.t: Reflection

Near the end of any long walk there comes an odd mixture. You want to arrive, and you do not want it to be over. You can see how far you have come, and a part of you would like to turn round and do some of it again. If today is your last walking day, you may know the feeling already. If it is not, you will meet it soon.

Bunyan's last scene is built on that mixture, and we should say plainly what it is. The river in the passage is death, and the city beyond it is heaven. That is how Bunyan means it, and he does not hide it. We are not pretending that the last day of the Camino is a death, and nobody who arrives at the end of a pilgrimage has crossed that water. But the shape is the shape of every ending: a stretch that has to be gone through, with no bridge and no way round. Some readers will have a loss behind them on this road, and this may be the day that touches it. Go slowly with it.

Look at what the passage gives. The pilgrims have been led to within sight of the gate, and between them and it lies a river, and it is very deep. There is no bridge. Two shining men who have walked with them say, without ceremony,
You must go through, or you cannot come at the gate
. They ask if there is another way, and the answer, a line later, is that only two people in the whole of history have been let by. So they go into the water.
At once Christian begins to sink. His cry borrows its words from the Psalms, and it is the most naked sentence in the whole book:
I sink in deep waters; the billows go over my head, all his waves go over me!
He is the man who fought Apollyon and walked through the Valley of the Shadow, and he is afraid in a way he has not been before.
Then Hopeful speaks, and his sentence is the plainest in the scene.
Be of good cheer, my brother, I feel the bottom, and it is good.
He does not say that he is not afraid. He does not make an argument. He says what his feet have found. There is a floor under the river, and it holds.

In the lines between, we are told what the crossing costs. Christian loses his hold of everything. He cannot remember the good things of his road. He is troubled by the sins of his whole life, and by the phantoms of hobgoblins and evil spirits. Hopeful has
much ado
to keep his brother's head above the water, and sometimes Christian goes under and comes up again
half dead
. Christian says:
it is you, it is you they wait for; you have been Hopeful ever since I knew you
. And Hopeful answers:
And so have you
. It is a better thing than a speech. Two friends who have walked a long way tell each other the truth in the water.
Then the turning. Christian hears a word that holds him, and they both take courage. He finds ground to stand on, and
the rest of the river was but shallow
, and they get over. On the far bank, waiting for them, are the two shining men who had led them down to the water.

There are two hard things to say. First, Bunyan's account of the crossing is Bunyan's, and it is a comfort he offers from his own faith. It is not a promise that all endings are easy, or a prediction. The terror in it is real, and Bunyan allows it. Second, the book's last page, which we have left out, turns dark: a man who reaches the gate without the paper he needed is taken away. Bunyan ends with a warning. We have stopped at the river.

What it asks of an ordinary day is something we all know and seldom do. When you cannot feel the bottom yourself, let someone tell you that they can. And when it is your turn to be the one with your feet on the ground, say so plainly, and say it while you are still holding the other person up. At the end of the road, and at the end of anything, the person beside you matters more than your own courage.
For the walk

items.t: Who has held my head above water on this road?

Choose one person who walked beside you, for a day or for a long way, and thank them by name. Say it aloud if they are near, or send it in a message if they are not. Tell them one specific thing they did, however small, and do not spoil it with a joke.

spans.t: At the end of the day

If this is your last evening on the road, it may feel strange. The day was a day like the others, and it ended, and the thing that you were walking towards is either behind you or next door. If you are not at the end of your road tonight, keep this page for the evening that you are.

Let the twelve days go past you, quickly, in the order they came. A great weight on the first morning. A bog that came on the second day, and a hand that came down for you. A gate that opened to a knock, and a burden that did not drop. A hill that you crawled up, and a bench halfway. A house where somebody asked where you had come from. A valley where a voice read out your faults, and another where you heard someone ahead in the dark. A town that sold everything. A smooth path that went wrong, and a key in a pocket. A high place with a shaky view. An afternoon in which two were better than one. And now the river.

Arrival itself may have been loud, or flat, or something you could not name. If you wept at an odd moment, or felt nothing at the expected one, neither was wrong. A threshold is allowed to be whatever it is.

Did the burden fall? You may know, and you may not. The book promised nothing about that. If it did fall, somewhere, on a day you did not expect, then say thank you, to someone or to nobody. If it did not,
be content to bear it
still holds. A road has not failed you because the weight is still there. It may be that it is lighter, or better understood, or only better carried.

Think of the ones who have held your head up. It might be a person who walked beside you for a week, or one who said a word in a café that made the next hour possible. It might be a friend by message, or a host who put out a hot dish at the right time. Hopeful's answer to Christian,
and so have you
, is worth taking to bed. Whoever held you up was being held up by someone as well.
You may find your first day without an arrow to follow a little strange. If so, it will pass, and it needs no explanation. Eat well, sleep on, and let the legs have their say.

All the bells in Bunyan's city ring at the end of the story. We will not say that any particular bell, in Santiago or anywhere else, is that bell. But a bell is a bell. If one rings tonight, in whatever town you have reached, let it count for you.

items.t: Who held my head above water on this road, and have I thanked them?
What do I want to carry away from these days, and what shall I leave here?
What is the plain bottom under my feet tonight, the thing I can stand on?

spans.t: A short prayer

For the ground under my feet, for the hand that held me, for the road behind me and whatever comes after: my thanks. Let me finish gently. Let the bells be rung for everyone who arrives, however they arrive. Let me sleep.

You have reached the end of the twelve days, or you have stopped early, or you mean to start again more slowly. Any of those is fine. This book was made to keep you company on a road, and a road has little use for a book once it is over, except to be remembered kindly.
Bunyan ends his own story with a request. He has told his dream, and now he asks the reader to make of it what they can.

paras.t: Put by the curtains, look within my veil, Turn up my metaphors, and do not fail, There, if thou seekest them, such things to find, As will be helpful to an honest mind. What of my dross thou findest there, be bold To throw away, but yet preserve the gold; What if my gold be wrapped up in ore?-- None throws away the apple for the core.

spans.t: It is a generous way to close a book. The author gives you leave to throw away what does not fit, and to keep the gold. We would say the same of ours. Some of these days will have rubbed, and some passages will have asked more than you could give, or less than you hoped. That is allowed. If a day did nothing for you, nothing has gone wrong.
What to keep
Not everything. Nobody carries a whole book. Here are four small things to choose from.

items.t: A step.
From the second day: when the ground goes soft and fear hurries your feet, go to the plain things first. Water, food, a seat, the next waymark. They were laid there for you.
A hand.
Give me thy hand
, says Help in the bog, and Christian gives it. Ask when you need to, and give when you can.
A key.
Somewhere in your pocket there is a reason, a sentence or a name that you forgot you had. Take it out now and then and look at it.
A voice.
The one ahead of you in the dark, who thought he was alone too. You may be that voice for someone else, and a greeting costs nothing.

spans.t: If you keep even one of these for a month, you will have kept more than most people keep from anything.
How to go on

Go back whenever you like. The days are short, and they were written to be read more than once. A day that did nothing in the first week may say a great deal in the fifth. Read them out of order. Read only the evenings for a week. Read one passage aloud on a bad morning, and nothing else.

You might also read Bunyan himself. This book has taken twelve small passages out of a longer story, and the original is in the public domain, in the same text we used: Project Gutenberg ebook number 131. Bunyan wrote a second part some years later, which this edition does not contain. Read it a page at a time, and skip what is hard. His own closing verse allows it.

And be honest about what you leave behind. Bunyan's world is stern, and a modern reader may close the book with questions about judgement, about the family Christian left, about the pages we did not quote. They are fair questions, and they keep.
A last word

John Bunyan wrote a story about a man on a road and called it a dream. He gave the road a bog, a gate, a hill, a house, two valleys, a fair, a castle, a mountain, a drowsy country and a river. They are the weather of a long walk. What he added, in the end, was company: a hand in the bog, a voice in the dark, a friend in the water.

That is worth taking home. You do not have to know exactly where the road goes. You need the next step, a little patience with yourself, and now and then a person at the right moment to say that they can feel the bottom.
Walk again. Next year, if you can. Or tomorrow, round the block, with your phone left behind and your hands open.
Bom caminho, and Buen Camino.
